newsitem.title: CANADA: CWB sees US EEP, world wheat supply pressing prices.
newsitem.headline: CWB sees US EEP, world wheat supply pressing prices.

text.p: The threat that the United States may use its Export Enhancement Program (EEP) and higher world wheat output were expected to weigh on prices in crop year 1997/98 (Aug/July), a Canadian Wheat Board analyst said.

"U.S. wheat exports and ending stocks are projected to increase in 1997/98 and the Clinton administration has asked for the maximum EEP funding of US$500 million for fiscal 1998," CWB analyst Larry Sawatzky told a CWB conference.
The U.S. last used EEP in July 1995. The European Union resumed subsidizing wheat exports in September 1996.

The CWB dropped its price forecast for benchmark No1 Canada Western Red Spring wheat for the 1997/98 crop year to C$160-C$190 a tonne. The range was below its range of estimates released Thursday for CWRS wheat in the current crop year at C$193-C$208.

"Due to higher projected wheat supplies in 1997/98 and aggressive competition among the major exporters, we are currently expecting milling wheat prices to decline somewhat in 1997/98," Sawatzky said.
World wheat supplies were forecast to rise one percent to 681 million tonnes in 1997/98 from 674 million tonnes this year, Sawatzky said.
World wheat demand was estimated to rise 0.35 percent to 570 million tonnes in 1997/98 from 568 million tonnes in 1996/97, he added.
World wheat trade was seen at 93 million tonnes in 1997/98 as well as 1996/97, he said.
World ending stocks were forecast to rise 4.7 percent to 111 million tonnes in 1997/98 from 106 million tonnes.

"Even though this may seem like a large increase for one year, world wheat stocks are relatively low by historical standards, so production shortfalls cannot be easily cushioned by a reduction in stocks," he said.
"This implies that there is considerable potential for wheat prices to increase in 1997/98 if production does not unfold as expected at this time," Sawatzky added.

The EU's winter wheat crop was in "very good condition" at this time with limited concern over winterkill and harvest expected to reach 97.4 million tonnes, down from 98.1 million tonnes in 1996/97, he said.
China's winter wheat crop also looked "quite good" now with output expected to be similar to the 1996/97 record crop of 109 million tonnes, Sawatzky said.
Higher output was expected in the U.S. and India, he said.
"Normal growing conditions should bring a significant recovery in output in Central and Eastern Europe, Kazkhstan, Russia and Ukraine," Sawatzky said.
"However, significantly lower wheat production is expected in the southern hemisphere in 1997/98...lower expected prices will likely result in lower seeded area," he said.

Asked how sensitive the market would be to a drop of 20 million tonnes in world wheat output, Sawatzky said: "I can't quantify it for you, but obviously a swing of 20 million tonnes either way would have a big effect on world prices and these PROs (CWB Pool Return Outlook).
